- When sentiment is consistently positive (≥0.67) over recent days, model tends to overestimate prices; reduce forecast slope or cap upward momentum.
- After sharp price spikes (e.g., >+5% from prior day), model often overshoots and fails to correct — apply downward bias correction in next 3–5 days.
- If sentiment is negative (≤0.33) and price is trending down, model often underestimates the drop — adjust forecast downward with steeper slope.
- Model exhibits strong mean reversion bias: if price is above 30-day moving average, forecast tends to overcorrect downward; if below, overcorrects upward — use sentiment to dampen correction magnitude.
- For 30-day forecasts, model often fails to capture sentiment-driven volatility — if sentiment swings sharply, adjust forecast range to reflect higher uncertainty (e.g., ±2–3% buffer).
- When sentiment is neutral (0.00–0.33) and price is flat, model tends to drift upward — apply downward bias to prevent false momentum.
- If sentiment history shows repeated “reversal” patterns (e.g., 0.67 → 0.00 → 0.67), model often misreads trend — use sentiment lag (e.g., 2–3 day) to smooth forecast direction.
